originalTitle: Perplexity's new Monitor API turns web search from a one-off query into a nonstop watchdog
author: Jonathan Kemper
contentHtml:
Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.

Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.

Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In August, The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks for an investment at a valuation of more than $30 billion, which means Perplexity needs to find profitable business models. The company is betting on agents like Computer and its always-on Teammates, along with developer tools like Search as Code.

originalTitle: Meta ads is now available in AWS Quick
author: Chris Geiger
contentHtml:
Marketers have never had more data to act on. Take an apparel brand that advertises on Meta technologies: campaign results live in Meta Ads Manager, briefs and creative assets in shared storage, and inventory, customer lifetime value, and in-store purchases in a data lake. Analysts export reports, merge spreadsheets, and rebuild the same deck each week, and the data ages before anyone acts on it. When the team does decide what to change, someone returns to Ads Manager to update campaigns, ad sets, budgets, and audiences by hand. As a result, teams judge campaigns on metrics alone, and the path from insight to action stays slow and manual.

Today, AWS Quick added a Meta ads AI connector. The connector gives Quick access to ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server operations. Meta ads customers can use natural language to create, manage, and analyze campaigns within Quick, while staying connected to the Meta ad management network. Marketers can complete tasks with support from AI, such as pulling insights to understand ads performance, creating product catalogs, and editing existing or creating new campaigns. Quick can also combine Meta ad management data with first- and third-party data sources to create dashboards, documents, slide decks, and automated workflows.

“Meta ads AI connector through Quick gives our marketing teams one place to go from campaign planning to execution. It lets us act on business insights directly in our ads, without the handoffs and tool switching that slow campaigns down. With fal.ai’s image, audio, and video models in the same workflow, we’ll test more creative ideas and spend more time reaching customers.”

— Tina Sang, Head of Marketing at fal

The video shows how to install the Meta ads connector from Customize > Connectors in AWS Quick, sign in with Facebook, and choose which Pages, Businesses, and Instagram accounts AWS Quick can access. It then runs two example prompts. One turns past campaign results into an eight-slide launch-plan deck. The other builds a dashboard comparing spend, leads, and cost per lead for two ad sets, with recommended tests to run next.

Connecting Meta ads to Quick and running prompts for performance analysis, campaign creation, and a shareable deck

Example use cases and prompts

The following use cases demonstrate how Meta advertisers can use the connector with Quick, along with sample prompts.

Use case What Quick does Example prompt
Plan and launch campaigns Drafts campaign, ad set, and ad settings from an approved brief. Flags missing budget and audience decisions. Runs a standard pre-launch check of naming, UTM tags, budget, and special ad category. “Using Meta ads, [campaign_brief], and past results, propose a launch plan for [promotion_name]. Flag missing decisions and prepare a review deck. Do not create or change ads yet.”
Analyze and share performance Tracks spend, CTR, and ROAS at the account, campaign, ad set, and ad level. Compares results to the media plan. Builds a weekly deck of top ads, weak ads, and next tests. Lets leaders review the deck and ask follow-up questions before meetings. “Analyze Meta ads conversions for [campaign_name], identify the biggest changes, and recommend next tests. Put the findings in a PowerPoint I can share with my team. Do not change budgets.”
Refresh creative and audiences Flags creative fatigue when frequency rises and CTR falls. Creates new Custom Audiences after approval. Compares the best-performing themes with competitor messaging and trends. Drafts the next creative brief with headline variants and an A/B test plan. “Use Meta ads results, [past_briefs], and approved audience information to flag possible creative fatigue and propose new messaging and segments. Draft a creative brief and test hypotheses, without activating changes.”
Measure lift and customer quality Helps plan a conversion lift study. Confirms eligibility and creates the study after approval. Compares lift with attributed conversions and customer value from the CRM. Presents the results, the level of uncertainty, and the budget implications. “Help me plan a conversion lift study in Meta ads for [campaign_name]. Check eligibility, prepare the inputs for approval, and explain how study results and [customer_outcomes] could inform our next decisions.”
Prepare product catalogs for catalog ads Builds a SKU sheet that joins catalog eligibility with stock, margin, and image status. Explains why Meta rejected items and updates product sets. Gives merchandisers one place to review rejected items. Routes items to data owners and tracks fixes. “Use Meta ads catalog diagnostics and [product_dataset] to identify ineligible products and image issues. Build a SKU correction table and propose products for catalog ads using authorized stock and margin inputs.”
Align spend with stock and profit Shows Meta spend next to warehouse stock and contribution margin for each product line. Models how shifting budget to high-margin, in-stock products would affect results. Runs scheduled stock checks and queues changes for approval. Applies the changes in Meta ads after approval. “Compare Meta ads performance with [warehouse_inventory], [margin_dataset], and [media_plan]. Propose where to shift spend and when a lower ROAS target could meet our approved commercial goals. Show assumptions and do not apply changes.”
Diagnose pixel, account, and delivery issues Triages pixel and Conversions API issues, such as drops in event volume and low Event Match Quality scores. Passes an Ads Manager error page into a troubleshooting flow. Gathers diagnostics, internal order counts, and Meta help articles into one checklist. Drafts a handoff email to engineering. “Investigate [issue] in Meta ads for [ad_account]. Compare available diagnostics with [order_dataset], find relevant guidance, and separate confirmed errors from hypotheses. Draft a troubleshooting handoff without changing the account.”
Govern spend and connect it to your data Routes budget increases above a set threshold to finance for approval. Tracks spend against approved budgets for each ad account. Reconciles spend exports with warehouse and finance records. Keeps budget policies, metric definitions, and spend reviews in one shared place. “Review Meta ads spend against [budget_policy], reconcile reporting with [warehouse_dataset], and use [change_log] to document known changes. Produce an exception report and proposed review steps, without executing changes.”

Note: The connector can make changes in your ad accounts. Before Quick creates a campaign, changes a budget, or runs another write action, it asks for your permission to take the action.

Before you begin, confirm that you have the following:

  • Access to Quick.
  • A Meta business account with access to the ad accounts you want to connect.

originalTitle: New in AWS Quick: More capable flows, an updated web experience, and agents that work together
author: Hillary Lovric
contentHtml:
Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together.

AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done:

  • Build, see, and improve business processes, all through conversation. Describe a process in chat and Quick builds a flow to orchestrate agents, skills, and tools with access to structured data, knowledge, and apps. New deterministic steps help make your workflows consistent and verifiable, now with longer-running workflows and support for large data volumes.
  • Triage your day and keep agents working in the Quick web app. The updated web app puts what needs your attention and a daily briefing on your home screen, adds the agents and skills you use on desktop, and keeps your work running after you close the tab.
  • Complete work spanning multiple agents through a single prompt. With multi-agent orchestration, several specialized agents work on your request at the same time, and Quick combines what they find into one response.
  • Bring more of your data into Quick. Connect to Meta ads and Amplitude, then ask in natural language and combine the answers with your other sources.
  • Skills on web, security and governance improvements, and more languages: Turn the way you do a task into a skill Quick can reuse, now in the Quick web app. Set configurable content safety and sensitive-information controls for user prompts. Support for Japanese, German, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), and Vietnamese.

AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away.

Turn one person’s process into your team’s process

AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most important work. Now you can build, run, and refine flows entirely in chat. And your flows can take on more of your tough work, whether you start it from the web, desktop, or mobile app.

For example, here is how flows could support a finance team. Maya is a financial planning and analysis manager at a retailer. Each month, she prepares a report for her VP of Finance that explains changes to costs and margins. For each region, she pulls last month’s results, compares them to the plan in a spreadsheet, writes commentary on the biggest changes, and sends the report. The process lives in her memory and a personal checklist. When she is out, a teammate has to rebuild the report from scratch, and it looks different every time.

With Quick, Maya can standardize the process, automate it, and make it available to her team. She describes her process in chat, the way she would explain it to a new employee. Quick builds the flow from her description and she tests and refines it in the same conversation. A diagram beside the chat shows each step, so she can confirm it matches how she works.

Figure 1: Maya describes her monthly report in chat, and Quick builds the flow with a diagram beside it. Both views, enlarged here for visibility, appear side by side in the same Quick window

A flow can now bring together agents, skills, tools, and data, and handle longer processes with more data. Fixed calculations and checks keep the results consistent, agents draft and analyze, and Maya decides what goes in the final report. On each run, her flow:

  1. Pulls last month’s results from the team’s monthly results dashboard in Quick, so she starts from the numbers her team already reports on.
  2. Works through several regions at the same time, so the report is ready sooner, even as the company adds regions.
  3. Compares each region to the annual plan in the team’s budget spreadsheet, using set formulas so the numbers are calculated the same way each month.
  4. Flags regions that moved significantly from plan, based on thresholds Maya set, and drafts commentary on each using the team’s commentary skill.
  5. Drafts a Microsoft Excel summary to the team’s shared Space and report email for Maya to review, and tells the team in Slack that the draft is ready.

Maya publishes the flow for her team. At the next month-end, she is at a planning meeting, so Jordan, an analyst on her team, runs it from chat in the Quick desktop app. There, the flow can use a spreadsheet of regional adjustments saved on his computer. Before the report goes out, Jordan reviews the draft, including why each region was flagged, asks for a few changes in chat, and approves it for the VP of Finance. When Priya joins the team, she runs the same flow at her first month-end, and the report is built the same way.

While this is a fictional example, real customers tell us they’re automating complex business processes to make them more consistent and repeatable. This gives their people back valuable time to focus on more strategic work. Take Pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider powering card issuance, processing, and payment operations for customers:

“At Pomelo, AWS Quick changed who gets to build solutions. Before, every analysis or automation depended on the data team. Today, people across every area explore information, make decisions, and build their own agents and flows within a unified, governed environment. Without growing our team, nearly four times as many people now work with data each month, so our data team can focus on its most complex, high-impact work. A single use case already saves us 80 hours of work per month. But the real transformation isn’t the hours we save. Quick is transforming our data and innovation culture: we’ve gone from a few people building solutions for many to an organization where everyone can create, experiment, and change the way they work. And we’re just getting started.”

— Rodrigo Marini, Head of Data, Pomelo Fintech Services S.A.S.

Get more done in the updated Quick web app

If you already use Quick in your browser, the updated web app puts the items that need your attention on the home screen as soon as you sign in. A reorganized left navigation brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together under Customize. It includes the agents and skills you built on desktop and ones others have shared with you. Your existing dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before, and you do not need to turn anything on.

  • See what needs your attention, then act on it. Your feed and a new daily briefing bring together the email and messages that need you, in priority order. Ask Quick about any item or have it draft replies for you to review and send.
  • Keep agents working when you step away. Schedule a task or start a longer request before a meeting, and Quick keeps working after you close your browser. When you return, review the results and respond to any agents waiting on you in Mission Control.
  • Find your work in one place. Library brings together your recent work, favorites, pinned items, and the documents and files you create in Quick. Your conversations, agents, and files sync across web, desktop, and mobile, so you can start in your browser and pick up on your phone or in the desktop app, where Quick can work with files on your computer.

Figure 2: The feed brings the morning’s email and messages that need a reply into one view

Get more complete answers from agents working together

Some requests need the knowledge of more than one specialized agent. With multi-agent orchestration, the agent you ask can bring in several specialized agents at once, each working on the part it knows best. The agent then combines their work into one response. Each agent keeps its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so the people who know that work best can build and maintain it.

For example, you might ask why shipping costs rose in one region. Your agent can bring in a forecasting agent built on your team’s planning data and a procurement agent built on the procurement team’s vendor contracts. You get one response that shows what each agent contributed, and you decide what to do with it.

Connect Quick to more of the tools your team already uses

Work lives in many systems. This release adds new connectors so Quick can pull from the analytics and tools your team uses every day. Connect once, then ask in natural language.

Meta ads. Create, manage, and analyze Meta ad campaigns in natural language through a connector to Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Quick combines Meta ad data with your first-party and third-party sources, and asks for your permission before it creates a campaign, changes a budget, or takes any other write action in an ad account. Try Quick free for 3 months and invite up to 10 teammates at no cost.

Amplitude. Ask about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion in natural language. Quick connects to Amplitude through its MCP server, so product and marketing teams can pull behavioral insights into the dashboards, documents, and workflows they build in Quick.

Connectors respect your existing permissions. Quick only shows each person what they already have access to. Quick asks before it takes any write action. Administrators choose which connectors teams can add.

Also in this release

  • Skills in the Quick web app. Skills are reusable instructions that teach Quick to do a task your way, such as reviewing a contract against your team’s checklist, or writing a project update in your company’s format. You can now browse, install, create, and manage skills in the web app, as on desktop.
  • Guardrails for prompts (preview). Administrators can set policies that filter content, block denied topics and words, detect prompt attacks, and protect selected types of personal information in the prompts people send to Quick. They can test a policy in detect-only mode before enforcing it, then apply it to individual users, identity provider groups, or the whole account. This feature is available to all AWS Quick customers subscribed to Professional and Enterprise plans.
  • Permissions and limits by group. Administrators can now assign custom permissions and limit profiles to groups from your identity provider, in addition to individual users, roles, and the whole account. For example, you can prevent your finance group from creating agents, or set how many agent hours each member of a group can use, without managing each person separately. This feature is available to all AWS Quick customers subscribed to Professional and Enterprise plans.
  • Choose which data sources people can add. Administrators can now control which types of data sources people can create, update, or share. For example, you can let people connect Amazon Redshift while blocking file uploads, or stop people from sharing data sources from a specific connector. This feature is available to all AWS Quick customers subscribed to Professional and Enterprise plans.
  • More languages. Use Quick in Japanese, German, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), and Vietnamese.

Every decision stays yours

Whether you build a monthly report, run one your manager built, or set up Quick for your organization, Quick works the way you do. Your data stays in your environment and does not train anyone else’s models. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals.

These features are available today in all Regions where AWS Quick is available.

To try what’s new, sign in to Quick or download Quick and get started in minutes. To learn about enterprise pricing plans, talk to your AWS account team.

About the author

originalTitle: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
author: Ravi Yadav
contentHtml:
Artificial Intelligence

Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks.

This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer.

Why a skill for KV caching and what can it do?

The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything:

  • A fit check before any spend. The agent reads your GPU fleet with a read-only describe-instances call and counts Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) interfaces. It asks only for what it can’t see: engine, model, tensor-parallel (TP) size, KV data type, server price, and how often prompts repeat. It stops and explains when something doesn’t fit.
  • Numbers from your workload. For short prompts, loading KV state can take longer than computing it again. Above a certain prompt length (the cutover point), the read wins. That cutover and how often your prompts repeat decide whether the cache is worth its price. The agent estimates savings from your own traffic with KVTrace, at no additional charge, and stops if they don’t cover the cache’s cost. Every number says where it came from.
  • Manage configuration across inference servers with the stack you already run. The agent adds the LMCache connector to your existing vLLM or SGLang engine, including vLLM workers under serving frameworks such as llm-d and Ray Serve. It keeps your routing and the engine’s settings and sets the servers in your inference fleet to one KV ID mechanism (hash and seed) and an explicit KV data type. Matching settings avoid key mismatches, where each server writes KV state the others can’t find.
  • Implements best practices. Before production traffic, the agent empties the local tiers and checks that two cache-loaded runs give the same output, because a layout mismatch can produce healthy hit counters and wrong answers. The skill guides the agent to seek explicit approval for high-impact operations such as creating, changing, or deleting resources.

Prerequisites

These flows, from estimating benefits to setup, require the following:

  • A coding agent that supports Agent Skills, such as Kiro or Claude Code.
  • GPU instances that support EFA RDMA write, such as p5.
  • LMCache 0.5.8rc1 or later and vLLM 0.11.1 or later (SGLang 0.5.13 or later).
  • ElastiCache for Valkey 9.1 or later, on cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes (if setting up the cache).

Flow 1: Can distributed KV caching help?

We gave the agent this prompt: “My vLLM fleet serves a legal assistant with 64K-token contexts on p5 instances. Returning conversations take 13 seconds for the first token because the GPU recomputes the full conversation history every turn. How do I fix this?”

The agent matches the request to the skill and, in Kiro, asks for approval before loading it. The answer identifies that the latency was caused by cold prefill, and three things in the answer matter for a real deployment. First, it checks for fixes that need no new infrastructure. If you turned off prefix caching, turning it back on can speed up back-to-back turns. If the GPU prefix cache hit rate is already above 90% with session affinity, you might not need a shared KV cache. Second, it identifies constraints specific to the legal AI assistant. A shared KV cache can let one tenant tell from response times whether another tenant sent the same text. Cases that must stay isolated get separate caches, and tenants that share a cache add their own ID to the KV hash. Third, it doesn’t guess the size. It asks for the model and TP size, KV data type, replica count and routing, and how long users wait between turns.

Figure 1: The diagnosis and proposed architecture for the legal assistant

Flow 2: Estimating savings

To size the savings, we gave the agent an example fleet of 8 p5 instances that serve 64,000-token prompts for a multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant. The agent looked up the GPU and cache node prices and derived the prefill rate and KV size from benchmarks. Finally, the agent recommended two cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes for distributed KV caching. The following figure shows the agent’s summary and the inputs it used.

Figure 2: The agent’s summary and inputs. It looked up both prices in the AWS price list and explains how it arrived at the recompute figure

We didn’t provide a cache hit rate, which is the share of recomputed tokens the cache would serve. The agent therefore presents scenarios and recommends a KVTrace run to identify the cache hit rate. KVTrace records the KV cache events from vLLM or SGLang. It then replays them offline against a shared KV cache of each candidate size. The recorder never writes token IDs or prompt text. Traces hold block hashes and token counts. Block hashes come from token content, so pass --anonymize-key-file when your prompts are sensitive. The skill records on every GPU server for a representative window, such as a full business day. The agent also notes that freed GPU time turns into dollars only if you run fewer servers or serve more traffic on the same ones.

Figure 3: The top of a KVTrace report from synthetic demo traffic. It recommends the smallest capacity that reaches 90% of the savings ceiling.

Flow 3: Setting up a distributed KV cache

We prompted the agent with: “Set up a shared L2 KV cache for LLM inference, starting from scratch.” Before it creates anything, the agent requests your confirmation to set up the suggested cache node count in your Availability Zone, at the estimated price. Once confirmed, it creates the right security group with EFA permissions, and a Valkey 9.1 cluster that uses a custom parameter group with caching eviction policies. LMCache gets its own cache user, with the password in AWS Secrets Manager. The agent prepares the GPU servers and starts one LMCache server per GPU server. Then it checks the cluster with a small test object and confirms that repeated prompts load their KV state from the cache over Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). On a GPU fleet, the skill checks the measured L2 share against the KVTrace prediction. For the full setup with every command, see Getting started with distributed KV caching in the Amazon ElastiCache documentation.

Flow 4: Troubleshooting

Prompt: “My LMCache server connects to the ElastiCache cluster and BLOB.RDMA_HELLO succeeds, but actual data transfers are failing. INFO largeobj shows rdma_write_errors climbing. What’s wrong?”

Following the skill’s troubleshooting guide, the agent reasons from the symptom pattern and identifies the likely cause as a security group that blocks EFA traffic between its own members. It provides you commands to check and fix the rule.

Figure 4: The agent explains the symptom, then gives commands to check and fix the security group

Get started

You can get the distributed KV caching skill or the AWS MCP Server from the Agent Toolkit for AWS. originalTitle: How Google Duplex evolved to also call businesses for you in Gemini
contentHtml:
Completing tasks like making dinner reservations or booking a hair appointment is time consuming. Live phone conversations move fast and rarely follow a script. The person on the other end can say almost anything, often revising their thoughts mid-sentence – and people often rely on subtle tone changes to indicate whose turn it is to speak. Pause half a second too long, and it sounds like the call dropped; speak too soon, and you end up talking over each other. Leveraging AI to complete these tasks respectfully over the phone required us to consider high quality speech understanding, contextual reasoning, and speech synthesis working together in a single, low-latency system.

We introduced Google Duplex nearly a decade ago to help address this challenge. Propelled by advances in foundation models, the Duplex architecture has evolved to power autonomous task completion across many core products, such as Google Search and Maps. This week, we launched Duplex in Tasks in Gemini App, a personal AI collaborator that can help coordinate real-world chores, like calling businesses for you and handling real-world requests on behalf of the user. In this post, we look back at the decade-long architectural evolution that made this possible — moving from early, closed-domain models to a unified stack built entirely with Gemini.

From closed-domain calls to Tasks in Gemini

What began as a narrow, task-specific system quickly expanded into a shared conversational infrastructure, built in collaboration with teams across Google.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, when business hours and services shifted rapidly, Duplex doubled down on verifying merchant info automatically to keep listings accurate. It remains an important data source; for example, business information sourced from Duplex’s phone calls had been shown in Search and Maps over one trillion times, as we shared in 2023.

Simultaneously, we worked with Android and hardware teams to bring these conversational models directly on-device. Starting in 2019, we rolled out new Pixel Call Assist features across five consecutive Pixel generations. These models continue to power features like Call Screen and Hold for Me, helping users filter unknown callers and speak with a live agent when a hold queue ends until the user rejoins. In 2025 and 2026, foundation models unlocked broader agentic calling in Google Search and Ask Maps, checking quotes, product availability, and service openings from pet grooming to auto repair.

Three generations of conversational architecture

Over the past decade, the stack behind these calls evolved through three distinct eras, moving from bespoke neural pipelines to a unified architecture using Gemini.

1. Pre-LLM closed-domain models

We started work on Google Duplex before modern language models and even before the transformer itself was invented. In these early days, to ensure businesses and users had a great experience, we constrained Duplex to narrow domains and trained custom recurrent neural network models on anonymized, task-specific phone conversations. Without pre-trained world knowledge, we taught our models how to handle every specific type of task efficiently. In practice, this meant relying on extensive training data for each task type — such as interpreting the rigid flow of restaurant booking versus checking holiday hours — to ensure the system could reliably navigate domain-specific logic.

2. Early generative models and hybrid stacks

Google Duplex started employing open domain foundation models in production as they emerged. For example, in 2022 Duplex used LaMDA in live calls. These pre-trained models simplified comprehension and common-sense reasoning, allowing the system to handle unexpected conversational turns and tangents, while remaining grounded in the context like a standard restaurant booking.

However, these early generative models were less predictable and sometimes slower than today's, so we built hybrid stacks that paired generative models for flexible phrasing with deterministic state tracking and strict policy guardrails. This helped ensure that both users and businesses had a great experience.

3. Unbounded tasks and Gemini integration

As foundation models advanced, we removed the constraint of fixed verticals entirely by shifting to prompting the system with free-text task descriptions. This allowed models to define a task simply via a prompt, enabling the system to generalize to new task types and nuances (like asking for window seating or extra space for a stroller) and new business categories, without building separate dialogue models from scratch.

Our calling stack uses Gemini to unify multimodal understanding, planning, and dialogue generation so the system can navigate multi-constraint requests — like scheduling car maintenance around calendar conflicts — and adapt when a receptionist suggests another slot.

Technical hurdles in live telephony

Even with frontier models, live telephony poses hurdles that pre-training on standard datasets like the web alone doesn't solve:

  • Pragmatic grounding for pre-call and conversational context, and real-world intent understanding: The web doesn’t have all the data needed to capture how calls unfold with busy merchants. Nearly a decade of experience with goal-directed calls helps our stack grasp pragmatic norms, starting even before the call. In practice, this means matching a free-text task with a business based on the historical context of past conversations (e.g., knowing a specific vendor doesn't take reservations for large groups over the weekend) to predict whether a task will work. During the call, this helps the model determine what makes sense to ask at a given moment, how to read polite indirect refusals, and how to keep calls brief and effective.
  • Sub-second latency in noisy acoustic setups: Calls run over compressed phone lines against loud backdrops like clattering in kitchens, espresso machines, street noise, and side chatter. Our stack is tuned for low-latency streaming inference so replies land at a natural cadence. Custom acoustic and conversation cadence models assist the core AI system with handling background noise and pauses, stop talking when expected, etc.

Designing for both ends of the line

Duplex has to work just as well for the business answering the phone as it does for the user. That principle shaped several design choices:

  • Clear disclosure. Every call opens by clearly disclosing that it’s an AI agent — specifically, an automated system calling from Google.
  • Businesses stay in control. Merchants can opt out of automated calls in their Google Business Profile settings, or simply say “Please stop calling my business” during a call.
  • No setup and zero adaptation. Duplex works through the phone a business already answers: no software to install, no booking system to maintain and no staff to train. Whoever answers can handle the call the way they would with any customer, even mid-rush with a line at the counter.
  • One conversation, many insights. Details gathered on one call can answer many later questions, so a business isn’t asked the same thing over and over. For example, Google Maps can show details that Duplex gathers about businesses, like happy hour specials, patio seating, pet-friendliness, a parking tip or even a weekly trivia night.

Conclusion

Many daily errands, local services, and urgent tasks still require speaking directly with another person to coordinate details reliably. By integrating Duplex’s capabilities into Tasks in Gemini App, we are taking another step toward closing this loop. Natural voice interaction becomes a seamlessly integrated modality that the agent can deploy whenever structured digital channels like online APIs or booking forms don't exist. Using our newest Gemini 4 models — including Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Neon — Tasks in Gemini can now support more comprehensive workflows like analyzing utility bills, processing transactions securely via the Agent Payments Protocol, and coordinating with users over email and Rich Communication Services (RCS). Through these capabilities, we are bringing this research into the next generation of AI assistance.

Acknowledgements

We’re thankful to the Duplex team and to everyone across Google leading and involved in this decade-long journey.For driving the transition to Gemini-powered calling and making this launch in Tasks in Gemini possible, we're especially grateful to Yoav Tzur, Sasha Goldshtein, Rafael Goldfarb, Liran Peretz, Ritika Pathak, Sen Li, Ran Manor, Dekel Auster, and many others across the team.

originalTitle: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm
author: Austin Cherian
contentHtml:
Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do.

We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance.

In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them.

A declarative foundation for Slurm cluster operations

We can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. The following figure shows the six layers.

Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration, administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database. HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it, minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests.

Automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them.

Introducing cluster extensions

The five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. As researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, and an exporter ships a fix. For this layer, lifecycle scripts have been the main mechanism so far, and they have drawbacks when the software keeps changing. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet. A mistake shows only when the script runs on a node, and nothing reports what’s installed, so nodes drift apart over time.

We wanted the software to be declared in one place, checked when you submit it, kept consistent across nodes, and visible afterward. In November 2026, we launched cluster extensions, which are software packages managed by AWS that you install, configure, update, and remove through APIs or the Amazon SageMaker AI console, starting with observability and user management, including directory integration, as the first software extensions. Compared with scripts, extensions have these advantages:

  • Validated up front: HyperPod checks an extension’s settings against its schema when you submit them, through the API or the console, so a misspelled setting is rejected before anything reaches a node.
  • Consistent on every node: HyperPod applies the extension to every node, including nodes added by scale-up or replacement, and keeps the nodes consistent as the cluster scales and heals.
  • Changed through the API or the console: You change a setting or upgrade a version with an API call, or from the SageMaker AI console, instead of editing scripts and replacing nodes. Both paths use the same validated configuration, and this post shows console screenshots alongside the API examples.
  • Visible: Each extension reports its status and per-node health.

Use cluster extensions when HyperPod offers a managed software capability. Use custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software or initialization that the available extensions don’t cover. HyperPod supports two cluster managed extensions today:

  • The observability extension (sagemaker-observability) collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), Slurm job, and Slurm cluster metrics and sends them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus.
  • The user management extension (sagemaker-user-management) creates users and groups with the same IDs on every node, controls who can use SSH and sudo on each node type, and registers users with Slurm accounting. It can also connect the cluster to Active Directory, for example AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory.

The following diagram shows how an extension reaches your nodes.

Figure 2: HyperPod can install, edit, or remove an extension. HyperPod records the desired configuration, a node agent applies the extension package on every node, including new and replaced ones, and health probes report status and health issues back

Using cluster extensions

You can use cluster extensions from the SageMaker AI console or through an API. On the console, the Extensions tab on a cluster’s details page lists each extension with its status, version, and ARN, and it’s where you install a new one. Each extension adds controls of its own, such as the metric store and an open dashboard in Grafana button for observability, and the number of users and groups and a Manage users button for user management. You can also manage every extension through APIs, from the AWS CLI or an SDK, to script installs, keep settings in version control, repeat a setup across clusters, or check status and health from your own tooling. The following table lists the six cluster extension APIs, from installing an extension to listing the versions you can upgrade to, along with console view for extensions.

Figure 3: Left, the six cluster extension APIs and what each one does. Right, the console view to add and remove extensions

The following diagram shows what happens after you call one of these APIs.

Figure 4: You declare an extension’s version and settings through the API. HyperPod validates and records them, applies them to every node for its role, and reports status and health

When you create or update an extension, HyperPod validates your settings against the version’s schema during the API call, so a misspelled setting is rejected immediately. It then records the version and settings as the desired state and applies them, with each node installing only what its role needs, such as GPU exporters on GPU nodes only. New and replacement nodes get the same state a few minutes after they start, and every node reports whether the extension applied and whether it’s healthy.

Updates send only the settings that you want to change, and HyperPod merges them into the stored settings. Problems that show up only on a node, such as a port or user ID that something else already uses, appear in the Health field of DescribeClusterExtension, grouped by cause with a code, a message, and a count of affected nodes. HyperPod retries internal failures on its own, and for anything else you fix the cause and call UpdateClusterExtension with no changes to retry the affected nodes.

An extension’s status is Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem, and Degraded when some nodes failed or report a problem. Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own sagemaker-user-management while a monitoring team owns sagemaker-observability. Each health issue names the component, describes the effect on your cluster, gives the next step, and counts the affected nodes, so you can see where to look without signing in to each node, as the following figure shows.

Figure 5: An extension’s status, and an example health issue for a node exporter that isn’t running

When to use cluster extensions and when to use lifecycle scripts

A useful way to decide is to ask who owns the software and how often it changes. Some of the software on a cluster is specific to your organization, such as security agents, license servers, and the storage layout your data pipeline expects. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs are the right tools for it, because only your team knows what it needs. The rest is software that almost every cluster needs, like GPU and job metrics and user accounts with consistent IDs and access rules. That software must match on every node and keeps changing, so cluster extensions are the better fit, because you declare it once, HyperPod validates it, and each extension reports whether it’s healthy.

The two approaches can coexist, but each component should have one owner. Don’t manage the same exporter, user, or service through both a lifecycle script and an extension, because competing configurations can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Cluster extensions work with every lifecycle configuration option.

If you already run these capabilities from scripts, you can move to extensions one capability at a time, and scripts and extensions can run side by side while you do. For each capability, the migration takes four steps:

  1. Call UpdateClusterSoftware to move the cluster to the November 2026 HyperPod AMI or later.
  2. Turn the capability off in your lifecycle scripts and upload them to your S3 bucket, so that new nodes skip it.
  3. During a planned maintenance window, stop and remove the script-installed agents on every node. This is the only manual, fleet-wide step.
  4. Call CreateClusterExtension to install the extension on the clean cluster.

If anything is left behind, the install names the conflict, such as a port that’s already in use, and DescribeClusterExtension shows it under Health. With user management, you keep the same usernames and user IDs. The following figure shows four steps.

Figure 6: Moving an existing cluster from lifecycle scripts to extensions, one capability at a time

What you need to get started with cluster extensions

You need a HyperPod Slurm cluster on or after the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later with continuous provisioning enabled. An extension runs software as root on every node, so treat CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension, and DeleteClusterExtension as administrator permissions. We suggest that you do not grant them to the cluster’s execution role, because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use its credentials. That role does need access to the destinations that the extensions use, which means Amazon CloudWatch or aps:RemoteWrite for observability and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the Active Directory secrets that user management reads. If those secrets are encrypted with a customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key, the role also needs kms:Decrypt on that key. User management also needs a shared file system, such as Amazon FSx for Lustre, for home directories.

For procedures, IAM policies, and configuration references, see Cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.

To see how cluster extensions are used in practice, consider a platform team that manages a shared Slurm cluster for several research groups. The team needs a reviewable cluster definition, GPU and job metrics, corporate directory access, local accounts for a partner lab, and separate ownership of observability and user management. The following examples show how the team configures these capabilities and responds to routine changes and failures.

Create the cluster from one definition

The administrator declares the whole cluster, including node roles, partitions, FSx mounts, minimum capacity, deep health checks, and the external accounting database, in a single CreateCluster request. For a complete example request, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI.

The request has no lifecycle configuration, topology file, or Slurm configuration file. Each SlurmConfig gives its instance group a role, and the GPU group joins the train partition. AMI-based configuration sets up the nodes, and the security team’s compliance agent is already in the custom AMI. The GPU group asks for 8 nodes and requires 6, so jobs can start as soon as 6 are ready while HyperPod provisions the rest and health checks each GPU node as it arrives. HyperPod selects tree topology for the P5 nodes on its own, and accounting writes to an Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database that the team owns. The administrator can still SSH into the controller node to inspect or tune Slurm directly.

Install observability

Leadership wants GPU and job metrics, so the administrator installs the observability extension. In the SageMaker AI console, on the cluster’s Extensions tab, the administrator chooses the observability extension, picks the metric categories and their levels and the collection interval, and selects one of two metric stores: Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. The following screenshot shows the install form with one store selected. The other option is available in the same field.

Figure 7: Installing the observability extension from the console, with configurable metric levels and a choice of metric store

The same installation through the API takes one create-cluster-extension call. The following example uses Amazon CloudWatch as the metric store. To send metrics to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus instead, you set the Prometheus destination in the same configuration.

The administrator installs the extension with one create-cluster-extension call:

aws sagemaker create-cluster-extension \
    --cluster-arn arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:{{111122223333}}:cluster/{{abcd1234efgh}} \
    --extension-name sagemaker-observability \
    --configuration-values file://observability-config.json

The call returns the extension’s ARN, which the administrator uses in later calls:

{
    "ExtensionArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:111122223333:extension/sagemaker-abcd1234efgh/sagemaker-observability/0a1b2c3d4e5f"
}

Whichever way it’s installed, each node runs only the components relevant to its role, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller. Schema errors are rejected before rollout, while node-specific conflicts appear in extension health.

After the install, the extension appears on the cluster’s Extensions tab with its version, status, and ARN. The screenshot shows the tab for a cluster that has both the observability and user management extensions installed, and both are Active.

Figure 8: The Extensions tab for a cluster with both the observability and user management extensions installed

Whichever metric store you choose, you can add an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace to the installation, so the team doesn’t need to build dashboards from scratch. After signing in to Grafana, they find two pre-created dashboards, Clusters and Jobs, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 9: The Clusters and Jobs dashboards that come with the observability extension in Amazon Managed Grafana

The Clusters dashboard gives a single view of your HyperPod Slurm clusters, built on the metrics that the extension collects and sends to your chosen metric store. At the top, it summarizes cluster health: instance count and health, GPU and GPU memory totals, vCPUs, memory, and Amazon FSx for Lustre capacity. It also shows the state of Slurm itself, including node states (idle, allocated, mixed, down, and draining), job queues, failed or preempted jobs, and scheduler activity. From there, you can filter by cluster, node, or GPU to drill into EFA networking, GPU performance and errors, and host-level CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics, as shown in the following screenshots. That lets you go from “is my cluster healthy?” to the root cause of an issue without leaving the dashboard.

Figure 10: The Clusters dashboard, from cluster-wide health and Slurm state down to per-node GPU, EFA, and host metrics

The Jobs dashboard moves from cluster-level health down to individual Slurm jobs. It ties each job’s resource to use back to the job itself, using metrics from the Slurm job exporter in either metric store. You can filter by cluster, job ID, job name, partition, user, or account, and see CPU, memory, GPU utilization, GPU memory, and disk I/O for each job, plus accelerator and NCCL metrics. That makes it easier to spot underused GPUs, stuck jobs, or communication bottlenecks in distributed training, as in the following screenshot.

Figure 11: The Jobs dashboard, showing resource use for individual Slurm jobs

Turn on deeper GPU and NCCL metrics

Later, a research team that is tuning multi-node training asks for more detail, so the administrator sends only the settings to change:

aws sagemaker update-cluster-extension \
    --cluster-arn {{cluster-arn}} \
    --extension-arn {{observability-extension-arn}} \
    --configuration-values '{"metricsProvider":{"acceleratedComputeMetrics":{"level":"ADVANCED"},"ncclMetrics":{"level":"ENABLED"}}}'

HyperPod merges these settings into the stored configuration and applies them to every node, restarting only the components whose settings changed. When the investigation is over, setting both to null returns them to their defaults, and at no point are nodes replaced or scripts rerun.

Fix a metrics delivery problem

One morning the extension shows as Degraded. A new instance group has an execution role that lacks aps:RemoteWrite, and describe-cluster-extension shows the effect:

{
    "NodeSummary": { "TotalCount": 19, "ActiveCount": 11 },
    "Health": {
        "Issues": [
            {
                "Code": "ExtensionUnhealthy",
                "Message": "otel-exporter-health: no successful exports in 5m6s",
                "NodeCount": 8
            }
        ]
    }
}

Once the administrator adds the permission, the nodes report healthy and the extension returns to Active, with nothing to reinstall.

Give people access

The user management extension manages the Linux users and groups on every node, and who can sign in and use sudo on each node type. You declare who should exist and what they can do, and HyperPod applies it to every node, including nodes added later or replaced, so no one connects to nodes or runs scripts to add or remove a user. Users come from local accounts that you list in the configuration, from Active Directory over LDAPS, or from both, and each group names the node types (controller, login, or compute) where its members can sign in over SSH and where they get passwordless sudo.

For the platform team, security wants corporate identities, with sudo reserved for administrators, and a partner lab that isn’t in the directory needs accounts of its own. The administrator declares both sources in one configuration, with group rules that say which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on:

{
    "sharedFilesystemMount": "/fsx",
    "userSources": {
        "localUsers": {
            "groups": [
                { "name": "cluster-admins", "gid": 3002,
                  "ssh": [ { "nodeTypes": ["controller", "login", "compute"] } ],
                  "sudo": [ { "nodeTypes": ["controller", "login", "compute"] } ] },
                { "name": "partner-lab", "gid": 3101,
                  "ssh": [ { "nodeTypes": ["login", "compute"] } ] }
            ],
            "users": [
                { "username": "admin-1", "uid": 2001, "groups": ["cluster-admins"] },
                { "username": "partner-1", "uid": 2101, "groups": ["partner-lab"] }
            ]
        },
        "ldap": {
            "ldapUri": ["ldaps://{{ad.example.com}}"],
            "ldapSearchBase": "{{dc=example,dc=com}}",
            "ldapDefaultBindDn": "{{CN=ReadOnly,OU=Users,DC=example,DC=com}}",
            "ldapDefaultAuthtokSecretArn": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:{{111122223333}}:secret:{{ad-readonly-AbCdEf}}",
            "ldapTlsCacertSecretArn": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:{{111122223333}}:secret:{{ldaps-ca-GhIjKl}}",
            "domain": "{{example.com}}",
            "useFullyQualifiedNames": "ENABLED",
            "ldapGroups": [
                { "name": "{{ClusterAdmin@example.com}}",
                  "ssh": [ { "nodeTypes": ["controller", "login", "compute"] } ],
                  "sudo": [ { "nodeTypes": ["controller", "login", "compute"] } ] },
                { "name": "{{ml-researchers@example.com}}",
                  "ssh": [ { "nodeTypes": ["login", "compute"] } ] }
            ]
        }
    }
}

Access is explicit, so after the extension is installed only the groups that grant SSH access, along with the default ubuntu user, can sign in. Directory users keep their identities and group membership in Active Directory, while the partner lab’s users get the same IDs, home directories, and the default Slurm root account.

The same configuration can be managed from the console. Choosing Manage users on the user management extension opens the cluster’s Users tab, where the administrator can add, edit, and remove groups and users, and set which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 12: Managing groups and users for the user management extension on the console

Upgrade an extension to get new features without AMI updates

When AWS publishes a new version of an extension, the administrator lists the versions that can be installed and upgrades in place without AMI updates:

aws sagemaker list-cluster-extension-versions \
    --extension-name sagemaker-observability

aws sagemaker update-cluster-extension \
    --cluster-arn {{cluster-arn}} \
    --extension-arn {{observability-extension-arn}} \
    --extension-version {{new-version}}

HyperPod checks the stored settings against the new version’s schema and rejects the request, changing nothing, if they aren’t valid for it. Otherwise, the new version rolls out to every node, and nodes that join later get it too. Upgrades only go forward, so the administrator picks a maintenance window. Any new settings or capabilities that come with the version can then be turned on with an update like the earlier one.

Scale the cluster and replace failed nodes

Before the end-of-quarter run, the administrator starts an on-demand deep health check on the GPU group and then adds nodes with batch-add-cluster-nodes. The request returns as soon as HyperPod accepts it, so the administrator follows it as a cluster operation:

aws sagemaker list-cluster-operations \
    --cluster-name shared-gpu-cluster \
    --status InProgress

As capacity arrives, each node is health checked, joins Slurm, takes its place in the topology, and gets both extensions with the same version and settings as every other node. If a GPU fails during the run, the replacement is configured and picks up the extensions the same way.

Review who has access

At the end of the quarter, security asks who has sudo on the controller, and the administrator answers from the API without signing in to a node:

aws sagemaker describe-cluster-extension \
    --cluster-arn {{cluster-arn}} \
    --extension-arn {{user-management-extension-arn}} \
    --query ExtensionDetails.ConfigurationValues --output text |
jq '[.userSources.localUsers.groups[]?, .userSources.ldap.ldapGroups[]?]
    | map(select(any(.sudo[]?; .nodeTypes | index("controller")))) | map(.name)'

The answer is cluster-admins and ClusterAdmin@example.com, and the directory group’s membership is audited in the directory. Because each extension has its own ARN, the platform team’s role can update only sagemaker-user-management and the monitoring team’s role only sagemaker-observability, while security has read-only access to both. None of these permissions belongs on the cluster’s execution role. When an extension is Active, ActiveCount equals TotalCount, and Health is empty, every node runs exactly that configuration.

Availability and pricing

Cluster extensions, including the observability and user management extensions, have been available since November 2026 in all the regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is supported, and the other improvements in this post were announced earlier in 2026, with each announcement listing its Regions. There’s no additional charge for cluster extensions. You pay for the AWS resources that you use with them, such as Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and AWS Secrets Manager.

Figure 13: The two extensions that have been available since November 2026

Conclusion

A cluster is easier to run when more of it is declared, validated, converged, and observable. This year’s improvements brought that to a HyperPod Slurm cluster’s definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health, and cluster extensions, available since November 2026, bring it to the software on the nodes, the layer that changes most often. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs stay focused on what’s specific to your organization, and the controller node stays yours.

To create a cluster as described in this post, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI. To get started with cluster extensions, see Cluster Extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Share your feedback in the comments or through your AWS account team.
